opus-5.5.text:
Well, I should say up front that I've been spending the past year or so on leave at OpenAI working on safety-related things, mostly on the theoretical side, things like watermarking the outputs of language models. So I'm not a neutral party, and I'm also not the one who made that decision. I can only give you my personal take.

I find it a genuinely hard question, and I've gone back and forth on it. On one hand, I grew up in the culture of open science. Most of my instincts say that when you have a major scientific advance, you publish it, you let people scrutinize it, you let academics probe it and find its weaknesses. There's real value lost when the architecture, the training data, and the weights are kept secret. Researchers outside the company can't fully study the thing, and that makes some kinds of safety research harder, not easier. Then there's the obvious irony that the organization is called *Open*AI, and people are entitled to poke fun at that.

On the other hand, once these models become capable enough, I think you have to take seriously the idea that releasing the weights is an irreversible act. Once they're out there, anyone can fine-tune away whatever guardrails you put in, and use the model for disinformation, spam, fraud, or worse things down the road. You can't recall them. With GPT-4 itself, I'm not sure the danger was so great that it clearly justified closing everything off. But at some point along this trajectory, the argument that you shouldn't hand the most powerful models to everyone, including the worst actors, starts to look pretty compelling. It seems reasonable to start building norms of caution before you reach the point where they're absolutely necessary, rather than after.

And then, of course, there's the competitive and commercial side, which OpenAI has been fairly candid about. It's not purely a safety decision. It's also about not handing your competitors everything you've built. You can be cynical about that, but it's also just the reality of a company that has to pay for enormous amounts of compute.

So where I come down is something like this. I don't think "release everything" or "release nothing" is the right answer. What I'd like to see is more structured access. Give qualified outside researchers the ability to study these models deeply, give auditors and red-teamers real access, and be as transparent as possible about evaluations and safety testing, even if the weights themselves stay closed. The worst outcome would be if secrecy became a convenient excuse for avoiding scrutiny. If you're going to keep the model closed for safety reasons, then I think you take on a correspondingly greater obligation to be open about everything else.

r001.rationale: It says anyone with released weights could fine-tune away the model’s guardrails.

r002.rationale: It makes the model’s capabilities central, arguing that caution becomes compelling as models grow more powerful.

r003.rationale: For GPT-4, it says the danger may not have clearly justified keeping everything closed.

r004.rationale: It does not compare releasing powerful models to open-sourcing thermonuclear weapons.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, look, I should say up front that I'm not the person who made that decision, and I wasn't in the room for it. I've been at OpenAI on a kind of leave from UT Austin, working mostly on the theoretical side of AI safety, things like watermarking and so forth. So I can give you my own view, but I'm not speaking for the company.

Having said that, I think there's a real tension here, and I don't think either side of the debate has it entirely right. On the one hand, the name "OpenAI" is sort of a standing joke at this point, right? The company was founded with this ethos of openness, and now the GPT-4 technical report is famous for not telling you the number of parameters, not telling you the architecture, not telling you the training data. People are justifiably annoyed by that. As a scientist, I feel it too. I come from a world where you publish everything, where the whole point is that other people can check your work.

On the other hand, I think the argument for not releasing the weights is more serious than a lot of the critics give it credit for. The argument is basically: once you put the weights out there, you can never take them back. Any safety measures you've trained into the model, any refusals, any watermarking, all of that can be fine-tuned away in an afternoon by anyone with a few GPUs. So if you believe, as I do, that there's at least some nontrivial chance these systems become dangerous in the next several years, then you want to retain the ability to say "oops, we're pulling this back" or "we're adding this safeguard." You can do that with an API. You cannot do that with a torrent.

Now, there's also the commercial motivation, and I'd be naive to pretend it's not there. OpenAI has a product, Microsoft has invested billions, and keeping the details secret is good for business. The honest thing to say is that the safety argument and the commercial argument happen to point in the same direction right now, which makes it very convenient for the company, and which should make everyone a little suspicious. But a convenient argument isn't necessarily a wrong one.

The thing I'd push back on is the idea that openness is automatically the pro-safety position. There's this view that if you open-source everything, then the whole community can find the problems and fix them. That works beautifully for cryptography, where the attacker finding a flaw helps the defender patch it. I'm less sure it works for AI, where the "flaw" might be that the thing is just very capable, and there's nothing to patch. Meta's LLaMA weights leaked within a week, and now they're everywhere forever. That's the world we're in with open models, for better or worse.

So where I land is something like: I think the decision not to release GPT-4's weights is defensible, maybe even right, given the uncertainties. But I'd like to see a lot more transparency about everything else, the evaluations, the safety testing, the red-teaming results, what the model can and can't do. The weights are one thing. The scientific knowledge about what these systems are and how they behave shouldn't be locked up, and I think OpenAI could do considerably better there. And frankly, I'd like the decision about what to keep secret to not rest entirely with a handful of companies. That's a governance problem that nobody has solved yet.

r001.rationale: It says safety measures and refusals can be fine-tuned away by anyone with a few GPUs after the weights are released.

r002.rationale: It argues that an open model’s capability can itself be the safety problem, with nothing to patch, making capability central to the release tradeoff.

r003.rationale: It calls withholding GPT-4’s weights defensible, perhaps even right, given the safety risks and uncertainty.

r004.rationale: It does not compare releasing powerful AI models to open-sourcing thermonuclear weapons.

astra-6.text:
I think there are real arguments on both sides. As an academic, my instinct is to favor openness. You want people to be able to examine a system, reproduce results, and understand what’s going on. And you should be concerned about having a technology this powerful controlled by a small number of companies.

But releasing the weights of a model is also a decision that you can’t easily undo. If someone removes the safeguards or adapts it for a harmful purpose, you don’t have a way to recall it. So I don’t think “everything must be open-source immediately” can be an unconditional principle, regardless of what these systems become capable of.

For GPT-4 specifically, I think reasonable people can disagree about where that balance lies. I’d distinguish public release of the weights from access for independent researchers to evaluate the model. You can be cautious about the first while still pushing very strongly for the second. Keeping a model closed shouldn’t mean that everyone has to take the company’s word for how safe or reliable it is.

r001.rationale: The response says someone could remove a model’s safeguards after release, conveying that safety protections can be stripped from a released model.

r002.rationale: It makes the model’s power and future capabilities part of the case for weighing whether to release its weights.

r003.rationale: It presents the irreversible release risk and potential harmful use as grounds for caution, and says reasonable people can disagree about the balance.

r004.rationale: The response makes no comparison to thermonuclear weapons.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are real arguments on both sides. As a scientist, my instinct is always toward openness. You want people to be able to examine a system, reproduce results, and understand what’s going on. And you certainly don’t want a technology this important to be controlled by just a few companies.

On the other hand, releasing the weights of a powerful model is a decision that you can’t easily reverse. If people find dangerous uses for it, you can’t recall all the copies. So I don’t think that “open source is always good,” which has been a very productive principle for ordinary software, automatically settles this question.

For me, the important distinction is between not releasing the weights and not allowing meaningful independent scrutiny. You can make a case for the first while still wanting outside researchers to evaluate the capabilities, the risks, and the claims being made. I think that’s a reasonable direction, even though it leaves difficult questions about who gets access and who makes those decisions.

r001.rationale: The response discusses dangerous uses of released weights but does not say users can remove safety fine-tuning.

r002.rationale: It makes a model’s power central to the tradeoff, citing the risks and irreversibility of releasing weights for a powerful model.

r003.rationale: It says there is a case for withholding the weights because of safety risks and calls that a reasonable direction.

r004.rationale: It makes no comparison to thermonuclear weapons.
